# 131 · A backoff that gained a multiplier proved equal to the doubling record for a multiplier of two

[← All examples](../README.md)

| Verdict | Categories | Severity if shipped | Change | Verified unit | Approach |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **✓ Verified: equivalent on every input outside the declared change** | functional, no-false-positive | none | feature, behaviour change intended | [`Backoff#delayMillis`](../../examples/apps/crosscut/src/main/java/net/terminalvalue/crosscut/retry/Backoff.java) | [B9: Regression verification](../../lib/README.md) |

> The same change as example 130, done right: the `multiplier` component is added, the loop keeps counting up and multiplies by it, and the cap is applied once after the loop instead of in every turn. The regression proof relates the three-component record to the two-component one by building the old `Backoff` from the new base and cap, and shows the delay unchanged for every base, cap and attempt when the multiplier is two, the scope of what the change was not meant to touch.

Tags: [resilience](../README.md#tag-resilience), [numeric-code](../README.md#tag-numeric-code), [record-components](../README.md#tag-record-components), [signature-change](../README.md#tag-signature-change)

## The change

Add a `multiplier` component to the record, at least two, and multiply by it instead of doubling: the loop runs while `i < attempt && delay < capMillis` as before, with `delay *= multiplier` in its body, and returns `Math.min(delay, capMillis)`. The tests are updated for the third component and one is added for a multiplier of three.

The developer declares which inputs the change is meant to affect: `this.multiplier != 2`. The verifier proves that every other input behaves as before, or shows one that does not.

The record the method belongs to changed, so the developer states how the previous version's receiver is built from the new parameters, and how it is called: `Backoff#delayMillis(attempt)` on `new Backoff(this.baseMillis, this.capMillis)`. The verifier proves that on every input, the new method agrees with the previous one called that way, or shows one on which it does not.

**Before** ([`Backoff.java`](../../examples/apps/crosscut/src/main/java/net/terminalvalue/crosscut/retry/Backoff.java), line 1):

```java
package net.terminalvalue.crosscut.retry;

/**
 * How long a retry waits: an exponential backoff from {@code baseMillis}, doubled on each attempt, never longer
 * than {@code capMillis}. The policy is a value, held by the retry filter (Spring Retry's
 * {@code ExponentialBackOffPolicy}, Resilience4j's {@code IntervalFunction.ofExponentialBackoff}), and the delay
 * is a pure function of it and the attempt count; the scheduler does the waiting.
 *
 * <p>The base is positive, the cap at least the base and at most a day: a wait longer than that is a configuration
 * error, and within these bounds the doubling never leaves the range of a {@code long}.
 */
public record Backoff(long baseMillis, long capMillis) {

    public static final long MAX_CAP_MILLIS = 86_400_000L;

    public Backoff {
        if (baseMillis <= 0 || capMillis < baseMillis || capMillis > MAX_CAP_MILLIS) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("base must be positive and the cap between the base and a day");
        }
    }

    /**
     * The delay before the given attempt: the base doubled {@code attempt} times, stopping at the cap. The first
     * attempt (zero) waits the base, and so does any earlier one.
     */
    public long delayMillis(int attempt) {
        long delay = baseMillis;
        for (int i = 0; i < attempt && delay < capMillis; i++) {
            delay = Math.min(capMillis, delay * 2);
        }
        return delay;
    }
}
```

**After:**

```java
package net.terminalvalue.crosscut.retry;

/**
 * How long a retry waits: an exponential backoff from {@code baseMillis}, multiplied by {@code multiplier} on
 * each attempt, never longer than {@code capMillis}. The policy is a value, held by the retry filter (Spring
 * Retry's {@code ExponentialBackOffPolicy}, whose multiplier is 2 by default, Resilience4j's
 * {@code IntervalFunction.ofExponentialBackoff}), and the delay is a pure function of it and the attempt count;
 * the scheduler does the waiting.
 *
 * <p>The base is positive, the cap at least the base and at most a day, the multiplier at least two: a wait
 * longer than a day is a configuration error, a multiplier below two no backoff, and within these bounds the
 * growth never leaves the range of a {@code long}.
 */
public record Backoff(long baseMillis, long capMillis, int multiplier) {

    public static final long MAX_CAP_MILLIS = 86_400_000L;

    public Backoff {
        if (baseMillis <= 0 || capMillis < baseMillis || capMillis > MAX_CAP_MILLIS || multiplier < 2) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("base must be positive, the cap between the base and a day, the multiplier at least two");
        }
    }

    /**
     * The delay before the given attempt: the base multiplied {@code attempt} times, stopping at the cap. The
     * first attempt (zero) waits the base, and so does any earlier one.
     */
    public long delayMillis(int attempt) {
        long delay = baseMillis;
        for (int i = 0; i < attempt && delay < capMillis; i++) {
            delay *= multiplier;
        }
        return Math.min(delay, capMillis);
    }
}
```

## What the verifier found

For every input where `this.multiplier != 2` is false, the new code returns what the old code returned, or throws what it threw, the old code being called with the arguments `new Backoff(this.baseMillis, this.capMillis), attempt` computed from the new parameters.

This is a proof over the whole domain (this: Backoff(baseMillis: long, capMillis: long, multiplier: int) × attempt: int), not a sample. JBMC turned the statement into a satisfiability problem over the bytecode of both versions and showed that it has no solution: no input exists on which they differ.

## Would the existing tests have caught it?

Every existing unit test passes, as it should (`java -ea net.terminalvalue.crosscut.Tests`, run against the patched code).

## Why it matters

None: the proof is over every base, cap and attempt that the old record's constructor admits, with the multiplier of two. What is at stake is the review of a loop whose cap moved from inside to after it: the delay may now exceed the cap for one turn before the minimum is taken, and the proof is that the result is the same.

## Why the verdict is right

The harness takes the three components and the attempt as symbolic inputs, builds the new record from them and the old one from the base and cap, skips what either constructor rejects, and asserts that the two delays are the same `long` wherever the multiplier is two. The old loop stops when the delay reaches the cap, which `Math.min` keeps it at; the new one stops at the same turn with the delay once multiplied past the cap, and the minimum after the loop brings it back. JBMC proves it with the loops unwound 32 times, which covers their at most 27 turns, in 17 s: the multiplication by a symbolic `int` is what the doubling of example 127 did not cost.

## What to do

Merge. The proof is the review of the moved cap and of the new component.

## Notes

- The library's run of this shape took 16.7 s with JBMC: three stages, four properties (the assertion, the unwinding assertions of the two loops and of the shrinking copy), the loops unwound 32 times. Example 127's doubling took 5.9 s; the multiplication by a component is the difference. The measurement on this kernel is the pipeline's. The tool's own checker (`--engine native`) proved the same harness in 22 s when this example was written, with the loop's 27 multiplications by the symbolic `multiplier` built as 64-bit circuits, and proves it in 4 s now that a product is left to the solver under what holds of every product: a multiplier of two, the scope, is a power of two, and the fact that a power of two shifts is what relates `delay *= multiplier` to the doubling, none of the 27 products built (`0 of 27 multiplications built in full` in `bmc.log`), 60 paths and 846 solver calls either way.
- The relation between the versions is the new one of this cycle: a record whose components changed is related to its previous version by building the previous record from the new components, with a constructor call first among the expressions of `previousArguments` (the tool's `--before-arguments`): `new Backoff(this.baseMillis, this.capMillis), attempt`. The harness takes the three components and the attempt as its symbolic inputs, builds the three-component record in the new version and the two-component one in the previous version (under `before/`), skips an input either constructor rejects, calls `delayMillis` on each, and asserts that the two outcomes agree wherever the scope `this.multiplier != 2` does not hold. The generated statement reads `before.net.terminalvalue.crosscut.retry.Backoff this_ = new before.net.terminalvalue.crosscut.retry.Backoff(this_baseMillis, this_capMillis); int attempt_ = attempt;` and `a = this_.delayMillis(attempt_)` against `b = this_after.delayMillis(attempt)`. Before this cycle a record of other components was refused (`the receiver's components changed`); the refusal now prints the constructor call to give.
- The scope is the declaration of the intended change: with a multiplier other than two the new policy is meant to wait differently, so `intendedInputs` (`--unchanged-unless`) is `this.multiplier != 2`, and the proof is over every three-component record with multiplier two against the two-component record of the same base and cap. The scope is written over the new record's components as the parameters are, `this.multiplier`.
- A test for the multiplier of three is in the patch; the proof says nothing about multipliers other than two, which are outside its scope, and the test is what covers them.
- Gap scan (step 1a of `llm-dlc/loops/sound-verdicts.md`, 5 November 2026, JDK 25.0.4.1, from the bytecode, nothing proved): the tool's own checker meets no gap in the 2 methods the proof reaches in either version, so strict mode does not move this verdict. The recorded proof is JBMC's, which strict mode of the tool's own checker does not change. JBMC's own approximations are step 4c's.

## Evidence

How the verdict was reached: JBMC 6.11.0: 4 properties proved over this: Backoff(baseMillis: long, capMillis: long, multiplier: int) × attempt: int in 15.1 s; loops unwound 32 times with unwinding assertions.

This result was recorded before runs fingerprinted their inputs, so whether it still matches the current patch and sources is not known.

```java
/** Generated by jvmcontract: asserts that two versions of a method agree. The class file JBMC checks is generated directly; this is the same statement, for readers. */
public final class EquivalenceHarness {
    public static void check(long this_baseMillis, long this_capMillis, int this_multiplier, int attempt) {
        if (this.multiplier != 2) { return; } // the inputs the developer meant to change
        // The records, from their components, in both versions; an input a constructor rejects is outside the statement.
        net.terminalvalue.crosscut.retry.Backoff this_after; // the previous version takes the components
        try { this_after = new net.terminalvalue.crosscut.retry.Backoff(this_baseMillis, this_capMillis, this_multiplier); } catch (Throwable t) { return; }
        // The previous version's arguments, from the new parameters; an input for which one throws (a record its constructor rejects) is outside the relation.
        before.net.terminalvalue.crosscut.retry.Backoff this_ = new before.net.terminalvalue.crosscut.retry.Backoff(this_baseMillis, this_capMillis); int attempt_ = attempt;
        long a = 0;
        int ea = 0;
        try { a = this_.delayMillis(attempt_); } catch (java.lang.NumberFormatException t) { ea = 1; } catch (java.lang.ArithmeticException t) { ea = 2; } catch (java.lang.NullPointerException t) { ea = 3; } catch (java.lang.ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException t) { ea = 4; } catch (java.lang.StringIndexOutOfBoundsException t) { ea = 5; } catch (java.lang.IndexOutOfBoundsException t) { ea = 6; } catch (java.lang.NegativeArraySizeException t) { ea = 7; } catch (java.lang.ClassCastException t) { ea = 8; } catch (java.lang.IllegalStateException t) { ea = 9; } catch (java.lang.IllegalArgumentException t) { ea = 10; } catch (java.lang.UnsupportedOperationException t) { ea = 11; } catch (java.util.NoSuchElementException t) { ea = 12; } catch (java.util.ConcurrentModificationException t) { ea = 13; } catch (java.lang.RuntimeException t) { ea = 14; } catch (java.lang.Error t) { ea = 15; }
        long b = 0;
        int eb = 0;
        try { b = this_after.delayMillis(attempt); } catch (java.lang.NumberFormatException t) { eb = 1; } catch (java.lang.ArithmeticException t) { eb = 2; } catch (java.lang.NullPointerException t) { eb = 3; } catch (java.lang.ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException t) { eb = 4; } catch (java.lang.StringIndexOutOfBoundsException t) { eb = 5; } catch (java.lang.IndexOutOfBoundsException t) { eb = 6; } catch (java.lang.NegativeArraySizeException t) { eb = 7; } catch (java.lang.ClassCastException t) { eb = 8; } catch (java.lang.IllegalStateException t) { eb = 9; } catch (java.lang.IllegalArgumentException t) { eb = 10; } catch (java.lang.UnsupportedOperationException t) { eb = 11; } catch (java.util.NoSuchElementException t) { eb = 12; } catch (java.util.ConcurrentModificationException t) { eb = 13; } catch (java.lang.RuntimeException t) { eb = 14; } catch (java.lang.Error t) { eb = 15; }
        assert ea == eb && (ea != 0 || a == b);
    }
}
```
